text: So a simple rain gauge is pretty straightforward. You have a funnel catching precipitation and directing it into a cylindrical tube. The top opening is wider than the tube so you get accurate readings. This difference acts as an amplifier. If the collection opening is ten times the area of the inner tube, an inch of rainfall fills the tube to a height of ten inches. This is so small amounts like hundredths of an inch can be read easily and precisely. But these instruments do have error sources. One is evaporation. The water you catch will evaporate quickly, especially in warm or windy weather. Another big one is wind exposure. Strong winds make turbulence around the mouth of the gauge. This can carry raindrops over the opening, so the gauge actually underestimates how much it really rained.
